system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
The patient was admitted on December 6th and passed away on December 21st, after being in the hospital for 14 days and 11 hours.

The patient had several serious health issues. They had heart failure (when the heart cannot pump blood well), for which they received dobutamine (a medicine to help the heart pump) on December 7th and 8th. There was an abscess (a collection of pus) in the left thigh and osteomyelitis (a bone infection) in the pubis (the bone in the lower front part of the pelvis). They also had Fournier's syndrome (a serious infection of the private parts). A drainage procedure (to remove pus) was done on December 3rd with the help of an ultrasound (a scan using sound waves) and a drain (a tube to remove fluid) was put in on December 15th. The infection was treated with ceftriaxone (an antibiotic to fight bacteria), as tests showed the infection was caused by a bacteria called E. coli that was multi-sensitive (meaning many antibiotics could kill it).

On December 16th, the patient developed septic shock (a very serious condition caused by a widespread infection) from a skin and urine infection. They were given polymyxin (an antibiotic) from December 15th, and amikacin and vancomycin (other antibiotics) from December 17th. On December 17th, an incision (a cut) was made in the intensive care unit (ICU) to drain a lot of pus.

The patient also had chronic kidney disease (long-term kidney damage) and needed acute dialysis (a machine to filter waste from the blood when kidneys fail) through a fistula (a connection made between an artery and a vein for dialysis) on December 16th.

The patient had a cardiorespiratory arrest (when the heart and breathing stop) with pulseless electrical activity (the heart has electrical activity but doesn't pump blood). This happened 10 minutes after a tube was put into the windpipe for breathing (intubation), following a report of slow heart rate (bradycardia). After 1 minute of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR – chest compressions and rescue breaths), the heart started beating again with a fast rhythm called VT (ventricular tachycardia) but with a pulse. This was corrected with effective electrical cardioversion (a controlled electric shock to reset the heart rhythm).

In the last half hour, the patient became unstable and needed norepinephrine (a medicine to raise BP) which was increased up to 1.5 mcg/kg/min. The patient's heart rate became very slow (bradycardia), the QRS (a part of the heart's electrical activity) widened, and the shock worsened. Because of high potassium levels (hyperkalemia) even after hemodialysis (blood filtering by machine), 2 ampoules of calcium gluconate (a medicine to protect the heart from high potassium) and 100 ml of bicarbonate (a medicine to balance body acids) were given. The breathing rate on the ventilator (breathing machine) was increased to reduce carbon dioxide (pco2) and thus lower potassium. Two ampoules of atropine (a medicine to speed up the heart) were given but did not help.

The patient then had an asystolic cardiorespiratory arrest (when the heart completely stops) and was in refractory shock (shock that doesn't respond to treatment). The doctor declared the patient dead due to no central pulses (no heartbeat felt), pupils that were fixed and wide (fixed mydriasis), no heart sounds, and a flat line on the monitor (asystole), as well as no brainstem reflexes (signs of brain activity). The body was released. The doctor requested contact with the family and was waiting for the death certificate to be completed. The cause of death was Fournier's gangrene (a severe infection).
